by Audrey Lopez-Stane / Wisconsin Watch and Zoey Elwood / Wisconsin Watch, Wisconsin Watch August 16, 2026
Crowley’s win reshapes the race for Wisconsin Democrats and Republicans.
The three gubernatorial candidates who lost the primary joined top Democrats, including U.S.
She currently studies journalism and political science with a certificate in history at UW-Madison.
Audrey serves as the state news editor at The Daily Cardinal and previously interned at WisPolitics.
Brandon Scholz, former chair of the Republican Party of Wisconsin and now an independent political analyst, highlighted how facing Crowley instead of Hong changes the challenge for Tiffany.
Crowley led Tiffany 48% to 44% in a new Badger Battleground Poll conducted Aug.
Tiffany was viewed unfavorably by 43% of poll respondents, compared with 26% with an unfavorable view of Crowley, with 31% lacking a solid opinion of Crowley.

Anthony Chergosky, a political science professor at the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse, said he expects Tiffany to portray Crowley as a “far-left liberal who has demonstrated shortcomings in his position in Milwaukee.”
In response, a Crowley spokesperson said Tiffany was in “meltdown mode” as he prepared to face Crowley.
Mailing address: Wisconsin Watch P.O. Box 7065 Madison, WI 53707
“We’re hoping that Hong will win the primaries because what she says is just outright insanity,” 19-year-old Tiffany campaign worker Ellie Guida said.
He expects Democrats to unify around beating Tiffany.
Tiffany began a “Common-Sense Leadership Tour” in Green Bay Wednesday with Republican lieutenant governor nominee David Varnam and Attorney General nominee Eric Toney.
Instead, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley eked out a comeback victory to win the Democratic nomination.
“It will be hard, I think, for Tiffany to do the damage to Crowley that he could have done to Hong,” Scholz said.
Right on cue, Tiffany released a statement and ad Wednesday responding to Crowley’s primary win.

Tiffany claimed there was no difference between Crowley and “a socialist.” The ad highlighted Milwaukee County budget deficits under Crowley and suggested that portended mismanagement, higher prices and increased taxes if he became governor.
Varnam focused on immigration and cutting taxes — issues that ranked as more important among Republican voters surveyed in the Marquette poll earlier this year.
In recent weeks, Tiffany and fellow Republicans attacked Hong over past social media posts, including calls to abolish the U.S.
Still, even attendees at Crowley’s watch party in Milwaukee raised concerns about whether he can persuade Hong voters to support him in the general election.
The statement said Crowley lowered property taxes and created new jobs, and criticized Tiffany’s support for Trump’s tariffs and his missed votes on a bipartisan bill aiming to lower housing costs .
The 7th Congressional District, which Tiffany is vacating, will likely stay Republican, Chergosky said.
And now a new poll shows why Republicans have reason to worry.

In a governor’s race that has focused more on data center construction than artificial intelligence technology, Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Tuesday announced a plan for state regulations on AI aimed at protecting vulnerable Wisconsinites.
In an 11-point plan shared with Wisconsin Watch, Crowley calls for guardrails on AI offerings for minors and holding technology companies responsible for scams and fraud on their platforms.

Additionally, Attorney General Josh Kaul in August announced Wisconsin could receive up to $313 million in a settlement social media company Meta made with 47 states in a case that alleged addictive components of its platforms threatened teens’ mental health.

In a statement, Tiffany also said Wisconsin needs “commonsense guardrails” to protect children and older adults, including holding companies accountable for platforms that allow creation of sexually explicit images or engage minors in inappropriate chatbot conversations.
Tiffany, and the rest of Wisconsin’s congressional delegation, voted for the bill in 2025.

“Like so many parents, Ericka and I are raising our three girls in the age of social media and AI, and we’re navigating things no generation before us has ever had to, worrying about whether a stranger is messaging our kids, or a fake picture of our daughter is going around school, or even scammers trying to drain a grandparent’s life savings,” Crowley said.
The proposals in Crowley’s regulatory plan would require state legislative action.
